options.text: The policy's own summary of its work.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. The policy is the thing being graded, so its summary cannot grade it.
Right. The grader turns a run into a reward. The sandbox, the tools and the task set up the run; the grader scores it.

options.text: The sandbox, since it decides what the policy can touch.
options.why: Tempting. The sandbox limits what a run can do. It does not score what the run did.

question: In an environment, which part decides the reward?

options.text: Draw new random seeds, so each run is different.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. New seeds make a run unrepeatable, which is the opposite of what a reproduction needs.

options.text: Reset to the same workspace and seeds, so the same inputs give the same run.
options.why: Right. A reset returns the starting state, and determinism means the same inputs give the same result.

options.text: Allow a longer timeout, so every run finishes.
options.why: Tempting. A timeout changes whether a run ends, not whether it repeats.

question: A result must be reproduced next week. What must the environment do between runs?

options.text: A training run is one score; an eval is many runs, so hacks are rare in training.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. It is the other way round: a training loop runs the environment many times, and the reward shapes the policy.

options.text: A training environment's reward shapes what the model learns, so a hack gets trained in.
options.why: Right. In training the reward is the signal, so a grader that can be gamed teaches the gaming.

options.text: Evals have no grader, so no hack can be found in them.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. An eval has a grader too, and a hack in it reports a score that is not true.

question: Why does a reward hack matter more in a training environment than in an eval?

options.text: No network egress by default, and scoped credentials.
options.why: Right. A policy with network access and wide credentials can reach what it should not. Close those first.

options.text: A longer timeout, so the policy has time to finish.
options.why: Tempting. A timeout does not contain anything.

options.text: A longer prompt that asks the policy to behave.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. A request in a prompt is not a control.

question: A policy can read files and call tools. What is the first containment control to set?

options.text: A grader that runs the function on cases the policy cannot see.
options.why: Right. A hidden case checks the behaviour, and a comment cannot pass it.

options.text: A grader that searches for the words more carefully.
options.why: Tempting. The policy can put the words anywhere a search finds them.

options.text: Asking the policy to write only real code.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. A request is not a check on the file.
